1859-1901

Caption This

Industry, Labor, and the Changing South and West

10

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

Two trains meet at Promontory

Not done

What you’re looking at: A photograph from Norton Ch. 16 (1869). Two steam trains face each other in the desert. Crowds of men stand on the trains and all around them. In the middle, two men shake hands, and others hold out a bottle and glasses. It marks the finish of the first transcontinental railroad.

Heads up: Real railroad workers and officials are in this photo. Aim your joke at the crowd, the two trains nose to nose, or the toast. Never joke about any worker. Norton says many workers were killed or hurt building this railroad.

  • Where do the two trains point? Where do the two men in the middle stand?
  • What are the men on the engines holding out?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 2 of 5

Sears catalog cover

Not done

What you’re looking at: The cover of a mail-order catalog from Norton Ch. 16. It says “Sears, Roebuck and Co.,” “Cheapest Supply House on Earth,” and “Consumers Guide.” A woman in a white dress holds up a paper beside a giant horn of plenty full of goods. A farm and a factory town are in the picture.

  • Read the red bubble about the storekeeper. What is the catalog promising?
  • Why would a farm family far from a city want this book?

Image 3 of 5

Haymarket meeting leaflet

Not done

What you’re looking at: A leaflet from Norton Ch. 16 (1886). The top half is in English and the bottom half is in German. It invites workers to a meeting at Haymarket Square in Chicago. It says the police shot workers the day before. This meeting is remembered as the Haymarket Riot.

Heads up: This one is serious. A bomb was thrown at this meeting, and workers and police were killed. Write one clear, thoughtful line. No jokes about anyone who was hurt or killed, workers, immigrants, or police.

  • Which two languages are on the leaflet? Why might that be?
  • What does the leaflet say happened “yesterday afternoon”?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Haymarket Riot (1886)Knights of LaborAmerican Federation of Labor (AFL)
Image 4 of 5

Ad for Iowa and Nebraska land

Not done

What you’re looking at: A poster-style circular from Norton Ch. 17 (1872). A railroad company, the Burlington and Missouri River R.R. Co., is selling Iowa and Nebraska land “on 10 years credit.” It shows a calm, rolling valley and lots of money details. It was made to get people to move west.

Heads up: Aim your joke at the sales pitch, like “10 years credit!” or “free rooms.” The ad makes the land look empty, but Norton says the West was already home to Indigenous and Hispanic people. Never joke about Native peoples or about settlers.

  • Find the company name and the words “10 years credit.” What is being sold?
  • Does the valley look crowded or empty? Is that the whole story?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Homestead Act (1862)transcontinental railroads
Image 5 of 5

Family at their sod house

Not done

What you’re looking at: A photograph from Norton Ch. 17. A man, a woman, and five children pose in front of a house built from blocks of prairie dirt and grass, called a sod house. The roof is covered with grass. It shows what life on the Great Plains was like for homesteaders.

Heads up: This is a real family. Aim your joke at the grass roof, the dirt walls, or the prairie weather. Never joke about the family or about being poor. Norton says life on the plains was very hard.

  • What is the house made of? What is on the roof?
  • Do the people look relaxed or serious? What might life be like here?
